9The original Fortress and the revival's resolutions

The skill every agent loads has a section, "Fortress as a language". Each of its points corrects a belief an agent may bring from its training. A part of the skill lists, under the same points, each place where the revival changed the team's Fortress, with the original, the resolution and the reason. This part tells it in plain words.

The team left three sources that disagree

The team did not leave one consistent language. It left three sources:

  • the specification, the text that says what Fortress is;
  • the interpreter (walk) and its library;
  • the compiler and its own, smaller library.

These sources disagree in places. The revival changes the team's Fortress for one of two reasons only: two of the sources contradict each other, or a program fails. It then follows the team's latest word that works: the compiler's library, the type group's later papers, or the specification.

Example: the number types

  • The team's interpreter library put the number types in a tower. A narrower type was a kind of the wider type: ZZ32 was a kind of ZZ64, and ZZ64 a kind of ZZ.
  • The prelude went from siblings to a tower and back in 2009. Christine Flood declared its widths as sibling objects in March. Jan-Willem Maessen made them a tower later that month. David Chase cut the subtyping between the widths in August. Sukyoung Ryu added the first exclusion, ZZ32 excludes ZZ64, in October. Maessen and Eric Allen widened the exclusions and added the first coercions, from November 2009 to January 2010. Guy Steele built the comparisons and the integer operators on the flat prelude in 2011.
  • In 2010 Justin Hilburn built the exclusion rule into the checker: no type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. In the tower, ZZ32 is both an AdditiveGroup of ZZ32 and an AdditiveGroup of ZZ64, which the rule refuses. The siblings obey it.
  • On 09-24 the revival made the interpreter's library siblings too, so that the checker accepts it.

So a model that remembers the tower remembers the team's interpreter library correctly. What it doesn't know is that the team's compiler had left the tower in 2009.

Left as the team had it

  • Functional methods: a method with self among its parameters is called as f(x).
  • Juxtaposition as an operator, and the whitespace rules. The grammar is unchanged.
  • Declarations: x = e, var x: T = e, x := e.
  • Loops and reductions are library code. A for loop, a comprehension and SUM turn into calls to library objects: a generator, which produces the values, and a reduction, which combines them.
  • Evaluation is parallel by default. The revival pins the suites to four threads in the build file, so every run is parallel and alike on any machine.
  • Only the compiled path checks static types. Walk checks more when it loads a program, but these aren't static types.
  • What the specification describes and the team never built is still unbuilt: dimensions and units, property declarations, regions, reduction variables, complex numbers.

Where the revival resolved a contradiction

Each item gives what the team left, then the resolution and its reason.

Dispatch on every argument

  • Overloads that differ in static parameters.
    • Original: the Working Draft says, in its overloading chapter:
      Although there may be multiple declarations with the same functional name, it is an error for their static parameters to differ (up to α-equivalence), or for one declaration to have static parameters and another to not have them. Hence, static parameters do not enter into the determination of which declarations are applicable, so we ignore them for most of this chapter.
      The 1.0 release of March 2008 doesn't have this sentence: it compared such declarations by taking their type parameters' bounds as supertypes. In git, the sentence first appears in the specification's sources as Sukyoung Ryu re-imported them in November 2009. Neither implementation enforced it. The checker implements the type group's model of 2011, from the OOPSLA paper of Allen, Hilburn, Kilpatrick, Luchangco, Ryu, Chase and Steele, which allows such overloads. The team's unfinished 2012 restart of the specification leaves the sentence out.
    • Resolution: such overloads are allowed, and the specification states the 2011 model. Appendix I quotes the old sentence. The reason: the implementations and the library already overload across static parameters, and enforcing the sentence would refuse about 180 pairs of declarations in the library's apis.
  • The return-type rule.
    • Original: the 2011 paper asks for the rule on every instance of a generic declaration. The checker tested one. A pair that broke the rule then passed the checker and failed the JVM's check of the bytecode.
    • Resolution: the checker tests every instance, as the paper asks. Such a program now fails when it's compiled, not when it runs.
  • How walk chooses between a generic and a plain declaration.
    • Original: the specification chooses by the declarations' types. Walk chose by their order in the file.
    • Resolution: walk now chooses by the declared types, as the specification says. A program's answer no longer depends on the order of its declarations.
  • fill and tabulate.
    • Original: the interpreter's library had two array methods named fill, one taking a value and one a function of the index. For elements of type Any or of a function type, both apply and neither is more specific. The checker refused the pair, and walk called a function meant as the value.
    • Resolution: the function form is named tabulate. Scala's Array.fill and Array.tabulate have the same two meanings.

Traits and objects

  • The exclusion rule.
    • Original: the checker has enforced the rule since 2010, and the 2011 paper states it. The Working Draft doesn't, and some of its examples break it.
    • Resolution: the specification states the rule. It keeps the examples that break it, marked "Not allowed". The reason: without the rule, the checker's return-type rule lets through programs that die with IncompatibleClassChangeError. The team's later texts keep the rule. The Types chapter of the unfinished 2012 restart restates it as "instantiation exclusion". The POPL 2019 paper, the type group's last published word, keeps it too: a class that extends two instances of a trait extends an instance below both.
  • What a comprises clause says.
    • Original: four passages of the Working Draft read it as a statement about types, and so are false for some programs it allows. The Types chapter of the 2012 restart reads it as a statement about values.
    • Resolution: every value of the closed trait is a value of a listed type. A generic trait may extend the closed trait without being listed, if each type that extends it is below a listed type. Read by values, the passages hold.
  • A trait's override, and object expressions, under walk.
    • Original: walk dropped an inherited declaration only where the object itself declared the override. Its load check of the Meet Rule for functional methods skipped object expressions.
    • Resolution: a trait's override overrides for every type below it, and walk checks object expressions under the Meet Rule. These are the traits chapter's rule and the Meet Rule's own wording, which names object expressions.
  • An abstract method without a body, and an override that overrides nothing.
    • Original: the traits chapter makes both static errors. Walk loaded both.
    • Resolution: walk refuses them at load. Five of the team's demos leave an abstract method without a body, so walk refuses them now. They're left unedited for the curator's choice.
  • What a type provides.
    • Original: the traits chapter says a type doesn't inherit a declaration that its own override overrides. The checker read every declaration of every supertype as provided, and refused the team's test disp0.fss, whose override widens a parameter.
    • Resolution: both paths read what a type provides as the chapter says. By it, the team's own test is valid.

Static parameters

  • The bound of a type parameter with no written bound.
    • Original: the Working Draft says Object. The library uses its generic containers with tuples, which Object doesn't hold, and writes Any where it states a bound.
    • Resolution: the bound is Any, because the library works only with Any. The compiled path keeps Object until the switch-over.
  • A type parameter that nothing in a call fixes.
    • Original: the implementations gave it the empty type Bottom, or left it unsolved, and some such compiled calls failed the JVM's check of the bytecode. The POPL 2019 paper gives such a parameter its bound: at run-time dispatch, the intersection of its upper bounds under the call's static return type, never Bottom.
    • Built: the specification states the paper's rule. The checker infers such a parameter at its bounds, never at Bottom. Walk gives it its declared bound, and leaves open one whose bound names itself, such as SUM's. Walk still gives Bottom in four narrow cases, among them a big operator's parameters with a plain bound.
    • Not built yet: at run time both implementations still run a dispatched generic declaration at the value's type where nothing fixes the parameter. Walk can't do otherwise, having no static types. The compiled path waits for phase 5, when its dispatcher will carry the call's static return type. A callout in the specification says so, and expected-failure tests hold the shapes where it matters.
    • Reason: the paper is the type group's latest word on the rule.
  • Sizes on the compiled path.
    • Original: the specification has size parameters. The compiled path couldn't carry them, but its code generator had a slot reserved for them.
    • Resolution: the revival fills the reserved slot, in the team's pattern for type arguments. This completes the team's design, and a program with sizes now compiles and runs.
  • Arithmetic in a size.
    • Original: the Working Draft allows a sum, a difference, a product or a power as a size, but doesn't say when two such sizes are the same. The checker refused any arithmetic in a size.
    • Resolution: two sizes are the same when they're written alike once each operation on numerals is computed. The library needs it: it writes a product in the storage of its matrices. The team's questions and answers in the appendix "Internal Document" set the boundary, refusing two overloads at T[\n+1\] and T[\0\].
  • A size known only at run time.
    • Original: reflect answers a NatParam. The team's clause comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \] on it was a comment, and the api's comment says that a NatParam passed where N[\n\] is expected makes n a static parameter. The checker refused every such call in the library. Walk ran them.
    • Resolution: the clause is restored, and the checker binds the call's size to the value's own size, as the team's comment says.
  • Comparing pairs and triples.
    • Original: the interpreter's library compared them lexicographically over element types with no bound, under the team's comment "Shouldn't these operators have to extend something? A,B,C?". Walk answered true for ((1,2),3) < ((1,3),0).
    • Resolution: each element type extends StandardPartialOrder, as the team did for the range points' own comparisons. Unordered deciding elements answer false, as RR64's comparisons do for a NaN.

Numbers

  • Tower or siblings. The example above. The one library now has the number types as siblings, as the prelude had them, because the checker's rule refuses the tower.
  • Conversion in walk.
    • Original: the specification says that a call converts its arguments when that makes it apply. Walk had a note "TODO add checks for COERCE" at that place.
    • Resolution: walk now converts the arguments, as the specification says. The revival did the work the team's note left to do.
  • Mixed number types in a generic call.
    • Original: neither implementation inferred a static argument through a conversion. The tower needed none: a ZZ32 was a ZZ64.
    • Resolution: the parameter takes the narrowest type all the arguments convert into. Among siblings, only a conversion joins two widths.
  • Overflow.
    • Original: the specification and the compiled path raise IntegerOverflow when a fixed-width result doesn't fit. Walk wrapped the result.
    • Resolution: walk now raises IntegerOverflow. Code that means to wrap uses the specification's own wrapping operators.
  • Ranges.
    • Original: the interpreter's ranges took any integer type. The prelude had ranges over ZZ32 only. The interpreter's library had no bounded range type of rank 2 or 3, and checked such a range against bounds by comparing pairs in dictionary order, so a subarray could read past its bounds.
    • Resolution: ranges are over ZZ32 only, as in the prelude, since a JVM array index is a 32-bit integer. Ranges of rank 2 and 3 got bounded types and are checked corner by corner, after the design of the rank-1 types.
  • SUM and PROD.
    • Original: SUM used catch-all operators on Number, under the team's comment "Hack to permit any Number to work non-parametrically". Those operators went with the tower.
    • Resolution: SUM and PROD are one generic declaration each, over the element type's own algebra, which gives the zero or one at that type.
  • Rounding a rational at an infinity or 0/0.
    • Original: the Working Draft gives QQ's floor, ceiling, round and truncate the result type ℤ, and a later paragraph says they return the argument at +∞, −∞ and 0/0.
    • Resolution: they throw DivisionByZero there, because the declared result is an integer.

Loops and reductions

  • Reductions without an identity. The interpreter's library lifted them to AnyMaybe and joined values at Any, while its api declared lift(r:R). They now lift to Maybe[\R\], the type the api and Set's Intersection already wrote.
  • A generator's size. Generator declared no size, though three library bodies read one. It now has a default that counts the elements, so "only needs to define the generate method" stays true.

Specified, but not built

  • A parameter whose type is left out. The components chapter says type inference finds every type a component leaves out, but no text describes that inference. The checker refused such a parameter at top level and crashed on a local function's. Now the compiled path refuses every such parameter, and the specification says so. This is the one error the checker count shows now.

Where the revival changed the team's own text, and why

  • The specification. 39 entries in Appendix I, each with a callout at the changed passage. Each change follows one of the resolutions above. The original sentences are quoted with their file and line, and the team's frozen copy is untouched.
  • The library. The interpreter's library changed most: 3.6K lines added and 2.3K removed since the tag. Each change is either one a resolution above calls for, or a slip the checker refused. The rule is to make each with the library's own devices, as it already does for the same kind of thing.
  • The team's tests and demos. 43 of their files changed, and none was deleted. The reasons: code meant to wrap now writes the wrapping operators (six tests); SUM is written with its element type; fill's function form is renamed tabulate (seven tests and the demos); numerals and shifts changed in UnsignedTest and two others; the ranges changed in RangePrototype.
  • Left as the team had it. The grammar, the evaluation model, the algebraic traits, the frozen specification and the full history.

Where the quiz was right about the original

A fresh model answered a quiz on Fortress from its training alone (part 5). Some answers the audit marked wrong are right about the team's Fortress:

  • The tower of number types: right for the team's interpreter library.
  • Arithmetic that wraps: right for the team's walk. The team's specification and compiler raised an error.
  • No conversion in walk: right for the team's walk.

Other answers marked wrong come from the team's own specification, which describes more than the team built:

  • Monoid[\T, ⊕\] with laws: a chapter of the specification. The library has it only in a comment and in its incomplete folder.
  • fortress run Foo.fss: the specification's overview says this. The team's tool runs a program under walk with fortress Foo.fss.
  • Complex numbers: named in the specification, in no library.
  • Tests that state their expected output: the team's compiler tests do this. Its interpreter tests don't.

Two answers are wrong for both the team and the revival: integer types that wrap by themselves (the specification wraps only with its own operators), and an Any type that doesn't hold tuples.

Fortress revival · 2026-08-19 to 10-12
# The revival so far
Updated 2026-10-12 for the curator, Pavol Vaskovic, and for Prof. Sukyoung Ryu. First written 2026-10-08. Dates without a year are 2026, times UTC. Each part ends with its sources.
## Nine parts
- How the revival treats the team's work
- The start and the exploring era
- The unsealed tree and batches 1 to 10
- How the record grew
- 10-04 to 10-08: the skills and the process
- Batches 11 to 13b
- Since 10-10: the study's close and the coordinator rewrite
- What the revival changed in Fortress itself
- The original Fortress and the revival's resolutions
Words used throughout:
teamDesigners of Fortress at Sun Labs, later Oracle Labs. Their last commit is a874948ac (2012-08-31).
type groupPart of the team that designed the type system and built the compiled type checker.
curatorPavol Vaskovic. He directs the revival and decides what is committed.
agentClaude session given one task. The coordinating session plans the work and launches the agents.
walkInterpreter. It runs a program with no static types.
compiled pathPath that compiles a program to JVM bytecode and runs it: fortress compile, then fortress run.
checkerStatic type checker. It runs on the compiled path only.
libraryFortress code that every program loads. There were two. The interpreter's is the one library. The compiler's own smaller one is the prelude.
switch-overPoint at which the compiled path moves onto the one library and the prelude is deleted. It comes when the checker accepts the one library.
recordFiles under explorations/ that hold what the revival has established (FACTS.md), what the curator decided (POSITIONS.md) and the plan (PLAN.md).
gap ledgerFile with one numbered row for each known gap or defect.
## 1How the revival treats the team's work
Why now. The team's work stopped in 2012, when Oracle Labs concluded the project. Its last commit is Karl Naden's write-up on instantiating generics at run time, on 2012-08-31. Pavol took the work up in 2026. His reason, in his words: "we're trying to finish what they didn't get time and resources to do". Frontier agentic coding systems have made that possible now. The project is his hobby, done with Claude in his spare time: "a personal learning exercise equal parts about Fortress as a language and agentic coding". Its main goal is a working compiler, so that one program, microGPT, a small GPT model written in Fortress, runs compiled.
### Custodians, not authors
The protocol of the work opens with this principle: "We are custodians of their language, not its authors." It asks the revival to finish what the designers intended, judged by the specification and by the library's own practice. Every agent is bound by the same rules through the skill it loads.
- No committed file claims credit for the revival.
- Where git doesn't record who wrote something, the authorship is rebuilt from the history. It's never guessed.
- Reasons go into commit messages and reports, not into the team's source comments.
- Every claim is checked against a primary source: the code, the specification, the papers or a command's output.
### The history, kept whole
- The repository keeps the team's surviving history: 5.4K commits on the trunk, from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31. With the old repository's twelve other branches, it's about 5.6K.
- It's a 2018 fork of a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. The conversion cut 146 links between commits, so git blame here credits whole files to 2012 snapshots. Authorship is counted over the full history instead.
- From that history, a map of who wrote what was rebuilt, with the evidence for each identity. The README sums it up: Sukyoung Ryu on the front end, from the parser to the type checker; David Chase on the compiler and the run time; Jan-Willem Maessen on the library; Christine Flood on transactions and the work-stealing run time; and a wider circle of students, interns and visitors.
- The map also says what git can't show. The project began in 2003, four years before the record starts. So Eric Allen, a co-principal investigator from the start, shows only about 230 commits. Two co-authors of the 1.0 specification, Sam Tobin-Hochstadt and Joe Hallett, show none.
- The team's frozen copy of the specification, which Guy Steele made on 2012-01-04, is untouched. It's the Working Draft as of 2011-02-02.
### Where the editing began
- The tag sealed-tree (09-16) marks the point after which the revival edits the team's language, library and specification. Its message sets the rule: each edit starts "from a failing test added to the corpus, with the full suite kept green".
- Before the tag, 28 commits made the 2012 tree build and run on current Java and Scala. 21 of them touch only the build and its tools. The other 7 correct the constant e, fix a name clash between the two libraries' System apis, speed up the suites and fix the specification's rendering.
- Also before the tag, five surveys mapped the system, down to where the designers wrote their reasons (part 2).
### Test first, judged by the team's suites
- Every edit of the team's code starts from a failing test in the team's suites. The fix follows, and the test stays.
- The check is the suites' own verdict, pass or fail, as the team designed them. A value that matters is asserted inside the test, with the suite's own means: an assert in an interpreter test, a run_out_equals key in a compiled one. No expected-output file is added. The interpreter's suite never had any.
- A defect that's measured and not yet fixed gets an expected-failure test, a file named XXX…, the team's own convention. The team left 56 in the interpreter's suite. There are 120 now.
- Every landing now runs the team's two suites and the specification's 130 extracted examples, with no failure. None of the team's tests or demos has been deleted. 43 of them were edited, each for a reason on record (part 9).
### Changing the team's text
- Each change to the specification follows the team's own ways of marking a revision. A labelled callout sits at the changed passage, as the team's 2009 draft put its decisions in notes at the passage. An entry in the changes appendix, Appendix I, lists it, as the 1.0 release listed its changes in an appendix. Each entry quotes the original sentences with their file and line, gives the reason, and says what going back would take. There are 39.
- Where the specification's early text and the type group's later, implementation-informed work disagree, the later work weighs more. That work includes the exclusion rule, built into the checker in 2010; the OOPSLA 2011 paper on type checking multiple dispatch; and, after the project, the POPL 2019 paper of Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu.
- The library's own practice is the standard. A fix extends the library the way the library already does the same kind of thing. No fix is designed from a reading of the specification alone.
- The type group's last paper is read at the source. Since 10-10 the POPL 2019 paper is in the repository beside its extract, as its open license allows. Gyunghee Park's talk on it is transcribed from the ACM video. The 24 worked examples of the paper and the talk were written as Fortress programs, run on both paths, and sorted to become tests.

How a batch works. A batch is one run of a workflow script.
- A rung is one piece of work, done by a worker in its own checkout of the tree.

- The gather folds each rung's notes into the record. A merged-diff review reads the combined change.
- The gate is the full check before landing: the build, both suites, compiled atomic programs at four threads, the ladder (below), and the checker's error counts. To land is to commit to main and push.

- The goal (09-16). Finish what the designers intended, judged by the specification as revised. The measure is microGPT compiled and running fast. The tree was unsealed on 09-17.
- Test first (09-17). Every edit starts from a failing test that stays in the suite (part 1).
- One library (09-21). The interpreter's library becomes the only one. The prelude gets no new declaration and goes at the switch-over. The rungs that added prelude names stopped, and the checker's errors on the one library became the measure.

The one library's nested number types broke it, so they became siblings that convert by declared coercions, as in the prelude. Walk learned coercion in batch 4; the library was flattened in batch 6. The checker's errors fell from 125 to 62.

77	## 8What the revival changed in Fortress itself
78	Changes a programmer writing Fortress would notice, by area. Part 9 gives the reason for each.
79	### Numbers
80	- The number types are siblings under Number, not a tower, as the team's prelude already had them. A wider type converts from a narrower one by a declared coerce.
81	- Fixed-width overflow raises IntegerOverflow under walk, as on the compiled path. To wrap on purpose, write ∔, ∸ or ⨰.
82	- SUM and PROD are generic. Under walk, a reduction whose element type nothing fixes runs. The checker still needs it written: SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#i] f(j).
83	- QQ is exact. A negative shift count shifts the other way. GCD and LCM are never negative. narrow keeps the low 32 bits. round sends an exact half to the even integer.
84	- QQ's floor, ceiling, round and truncate throw DivisionByZero at +∞, −∞ and 0/0.
85	- The library's numeral type is IntLiteral, a sibling every number type converts from. Walk's numerals are unchanged for now.
86	### Ranges
87	- Ranges are over ZZ32 only. A range over ZZ64, NN32, NN64 or ZZ stops when built.
88	- Ranges of rank 2 and 3 have bounded types of their own, BoundedRange2D and BoundedRange3D. #(0,n) is empty.
89	- An array subscript of rank 2 or 3 is checked corner by corner, so a corner outside the bounds raises IndexOutOfBounds.
90	- The open range (:) can't be cut: its truncL, truncR, every, imposeStride and atMost fail.
91	### Arrays and the rest of the library
92	- fill takes a value; tabulate takes a function.
93	- The array types bound their elements: T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }.
94	- String's left and right answer Just of a character, or Nothing. String's juxtaposition is three top-level operators.
95	- Pairs and triples compare only elements that have an order. Under walk, (1,2) < (1,2.5) is refused.
96	- A reduction without an identity lifts to Maybe[\R\].
97	- Every generator has a size. The default counts its elements.
98	- Array storage is still boxed.
99	### Walk
100	- Walk converts by coercion at calls, bindings and assignments, picking the coercion from the run-time value.
101	- Walk infers type arguments through coercions. A type parameter nothing fixes takes its bound, and one whose bound names itself stays open.
102	- Walk chooses between a generic and a plain declaration by declared types, not by order in the file.
103	- A trait's override overrides for every type below it.
104	- At load, walk refuses some programs it used to run: an object extending two closed traits without being listed; two functional methods with no declaration on their meet, in generic types and object expressions too; an object that leaves an inherited abstract method without a body; an override that overrides nothing.

126	## 9The original Fortress and the revival's resolutions
127	The skill every agent loads has a section, "Fortress as a language". Each of its points corrects a belief an agent may bring from its training. A part of the skill lists, under the same points, each place where the revival changed the team's Fortress, with the original, the resolution and the reason. This part tells it in plain words.
128	### The team left three sources that disagree
129	The team did not leave one consistent language. It left three sources:
130	- the specification, the text that says what Fortress is;
131	- the interpreter (walk) and its library;

132	- the compiler and its own, smaller library.
133	These sources disagree in places. The revival changes the team's Fortress for one of two reasons only: two of the sources contradict each other, or a program fails. It then follows the team's latest word that works: the compiler's library, the type group's later papers, or the specification.
134	### Example: the number types
135	- The team's interpreter library put the number types in a tower. A narrower type was a kind of the wider type: ZZ32 was a kind of ZZ64, and ZZ64 a kind of ZZ.
136	- The prelude went from siblings to a tower and back in 2009. Christine Flood declared its widths as sibling objects in March. Jan-Willem Maessen made them a tower later that month. David Chase cut the subtyping between the widths in August. Sukyoung Ryu added the first exclusion, ZZ32 excludes ZZ64, in October. Maessen and Eric Allen widened the exclusions and added the first coercions, from November 2009 to January 2010. Guy Steele built the comparisons and the integer operators on the flat prelude in 2011.
137	- In 2010 Justin Hilburn built the exclusion rule into the checker: no type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. In the tower, ZZ32 is both an AdditiveGroup of ZZ32 and an AdditiveGroup of ZZ64, which the rule refuses. The siblings obey it.
138	- On 09-24 the revival made the interpreter's library siblings too, so that the checker accepts it.
139	So a model that remembers the tower remembers the team's interpreter library correctly. What it doesn't know is that the team's compiler had left the tower in 2009.
140	### Left as the team had it
141	- Functional methods: a method with self among its parameters is called as f(x).
142	- Juxtaposition as an operator, and the whitespace rules. The grammar is unchanged.
143	- Declarations: x = e, var x: T = e, x := e.
144	- Loops and reductions are library code. A for loop, a comprehension and SUM turn into calls to library objects: a generator, which produces the values, and a reduction, which combines them.
145	- Evaluation is parallel by default. The revival pins the suites to four threads in the build file, so every run is parallel and alike on any machine.
146	- Only the compiled path checks static types. Walk checks more when it loads a program, but these aren't static types.
147	- What the specification describes and the team never built is still unbuilt: dimensions and units, property declarations, regions, reduction variables, complex numbers.
148	### Where the revival resolved a contradiction
149	Each item gives what the team left, then the resolution and its reason.
150	#### Dispatch on every argument
151	- Overloads that differ in static parameters.
152	- Original: the Working Draft says, in its overloading chapter:
153	Although there may be multiple declarations with the same functional name, it is an error for their static parameters to differ (up to α-equivalence), or for one declaration to have static parameters and another to not have them. Hence, static parameters do not enter into the determination of which declarations are applicable, so we ignore them for most of this chapter.
154	The 1.0 release of March 2008 doesn't have this sentence: it compared such declarations by taking their type parameters' bounds as supertypes. In git, the sentence first appears in the specification's sources as Sukyoung Ryu re-imported them in November 2009. Neither implementation enforced it. The checker implements the type group's model of 2011, from the OOPSLA paper of Allen, Hilburn, Kilpatrick, Luchangco, Ryu, Chase and Steele, which allows such overloads. The team's unfinished 2012 restart of the specification leaves the sentence out.
155	- Resolution: such overloads are allowed, and the specification states the 2011 model. Appendix I quotes the old sentence. The reason: the implementations and the library already overload across static parameters, and enforcing the sentence would refuse about 180 pairs of declarations in the library's apis.
156	- The return-type rule.
157	- Original: the 2011 paper asks for the rule on every instance of a generic declaration. The checker tested one. A pair that broke the rule then passed the checker and failed the JVM's check of the bytecode.
158	- Resolution: the checker tests every instance, as the paper asks. Such a program now fails when it's compiled, not when it runs.
159	- How walk chooses between a generic and a plain declaration.
160	- Original: the specification chooses by the declarations' types. Walk chose by their order in the file.
161	- Resolution: walk now chooses by the declared types, as the specification says. A program's answer no longer depends on the order of its declarations.
162	- fill and tabulate.
163	- Original: the interpreter's library had two array methods named fill, one taking a value and one a function of the index. For elements of type Any or of a function type, both apply and neither is more specific. The checker refused the pair, and walk called a function meant as the value.
164	- Resolution: the function form is named tabulate. Scala's Array.fill and Array.tabulate have the same two meanings.
165	#### Traits and objects
166	- The exclusion rule.
167	- Original: the checker has enforced the rule since 2010, and the 2011 paper states it. The Working Draft doesn't, and some of its examples break it.
168	- Resolution: the specification states the rule. It keeps the examples that break it, marked "Not allowed". The reason: without the rule, the checker's return-type rule lets through programs that die with IncompatibleClassChangeError. The team's later texts keep the rule. The Types chapter of the unfinished 2012 restart restates it as "instantiation exclusion". The POPL 2019 paper, the type group's last published word, keeps it too: a class that extends two instances of a trait extends an instance below both.
169	- What a comprises clause says.
170	- Original: four passages of the Working Draft read it as a statement about types, and so are false for some programs it allows. The Types chapter of the 2012 restart reads it as a statement about values.
171	- Resolution: every value of the closed trait is a value of a listed type. A generic trait may extend the closed trait without being listed, if each type that extends it is below a listed type. Read by values, the passages hold.
172	- A trait's override, and object expressions, under walk.
173	- Original: walk dropped an inherited declaration only where the object itself declared the override. Its load check of the Meet Rule for functional methods skipped object expressions.
174	- Resolution: a trait's override overrides for every type below it, and walk checks object expressions under the Meet Rule. These are the traits chapter's rule and the Meet Rule's own wording, which names object expressions.
175	- An abstract method without a body, and an override that overrides nothing.
176	- Original: the traits chapter makes both static errors. Walk loaded both.
177	- Resolution: walk refuses them at load. Five of the team's demos leave an abstract method without a body, so walk refuses them now. They're left unedited for the curator's choice.
178	- What a type provides.
179	- Original: the traits chapter says a type doesn't inherit a declaration that its own override overrides. The checker read every declaration of every supertype as provided, and refused the team's test disp0.fss, whose override widens a parameter.
180	- Resolution: both paths read what a type provides as the chapter says. By it, the team's own test is valid.
181	#### Static parameters
182	- The bound of a type parameter with no written bound.
183	- Original: the Working Draft says Object. The library uses its generic containers with tuples, which Object doesn't hold, and writes Any where it states a bound.
184	- Resolution: the bound is Any, because the library works only with Any. The compiled path keeps Object until the switch-over.
185	- A type parameter that nothing in a call fixes.
186	- Original: the implementations gave it the empty type Bottom, or left it unsolved, and some such compiled calls failed the JVM's check of the bytecode. The POPL 2019 paper gives such a parameter its bound: at run-time dispatch, the intersection of its upper bounds under the call's static return type, never Bottom.
187	- Built: the specification states the paper's rule. The checker infers such a parameter at its bounds, never at Bottom. Walk gives it its declared bound, and leaves open one whose bound names itself, such as SUM's. Walk still gives Bottom in four narrow cases, among them a big operator's parameters with a plain bound.
188	- Not built yet: at run time both implementations still run a dispatched generic declaration at the value's type where nothing fixes the parameter. Walk can't do otherwise, having no static types. The compiled path waits for phase 5, when its dispatcher will carry the call's static return type. A callout in the specification says so, and expected-failure tests hold the shapes where it matters.
189	- Reason: the paper is the type group's latest word on the rule.
190	- Sizes on the compiled path.
191	- Original: the specification has size parameters. The compiled path couldn't carry them, but its code generator had a slot reserved for them.
192	- Resolution: the revival fills the reserved slot, in the team's pattern for type arguments. This completes the team's design, and a program with sizes now compiles and runs.
193	- Arithmetic in a size.
194	- Original: the Working Draft allows a sum, a difference, a product or a power as a size, but doesn't say when two such sizes are the same. The checker refused any arithmetic in a size.
195	- Resolution: two sizes are the same when they're written alike once each operation on numerals is computed, and a size with a static parameter in it isn't known to differ from a numeral. The library needs the first: it writes a product in the storage of its matrices. The team's questions and answers in the appendix "Internal Document" give the second: they refuse two overloads at T[\n+1\] and T[\0\].
196	- A size known only at run time.
197	- Original: reflect answers a NatParam. The team's clause comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \] on it was a comment, and the api's comment says that a NatParam passed where N[\n\] is expected makes n a static parameter. The checker refused every such call in the library. Walk ran them.
198	- Resolution: the clause is restored, and the checker binds the call's size to the value's own size, as the team's comment says.
199	- Comparing pairs and triples.
200	- Original: the interpreter's library compared them lexicographically over element types with no bound, under the team's comment "Shouldn't these operators have to extend something? A,B,C?". Walk answered true for ((1,2),3) < ((1,3),0).
201	- Resolution: each element type extends StandardPartialOrder, as the team did for the range points' own comparisons. Unordered deciding elements answer false, as RR64's comparisons do for a NaN.
202	#### Numbers
203	- Tower or siblings. The example above. The one library now has the number types as siblings, as the prelude had them, because the checker's rule refuses the tower.
204	- Conversion in walk.
205	- Original: the specification says that a call converts its arguments when that makes it apply. Walk had a note "TODO add checks for COERCE" at that place.
206	- Resolution: walk now converts the arguments, as the specification says. The revival did the work the team's note left to do.
207	- Mixed number types in a generic call.
208	- Original: neither implementation inferred a static argument through a conversion. The tower needed none: a ZZ32 was a ZZ64.
209	- Resolution: the parameter takes the narrowest type all the arguments convert into. Among siblings, only a conversion joins two widths.
210	- Overflow.
211	- Original: the specification and the compiled path raise IntegerOverflow when a fixed-width result doesn't fit. Walk wrapped the result.
212	- Resolution: walk now raises IntegerOverflow. Code that means to wrap uses the specification's own wrapping operators.
213	- Ranges.
214	- Original: the interpreter's ranges took any integer type. The prelude had ranges over ZZ32 only. The interpreter's library had no bounded range type of rank 2 or 3, and checked such a range against bounds by comparing pairs in dictionary order, so a subarray could read past its bounds.
215	- Resolution: ranges are over ZZ32 only, as in the prelude, since a JVM array index is a 32-bit integer. Ranges of rank 2 and 3 got bounded types and are checked corner by corner, after the design of the rank-1 types.
216	- SUM and PROD.
217	- Original: SUM used catch-all operators on Number, under the team's comment "Hack to permit any Number to work non-parametrically". Those operators went with the tower.
218	- Resolution: SUM and PROD are one generic declaration each, over the element type's own algebra, which gives the zero or one at that type.
219	- Rounding a rational at an infinity or 0/0.
220	- Original: the Working Draft gives QQ's floor, ceiling, round and truncate the result type ℤ, and a later paragraph says they return the argument at +∞, −∞ and 0/0.
221	- Resolution: they throw DivisionByZero there, because the declared result is an integer.
222	#### Loops and reductions
223	- Reductions without an identity. The interpreter's library lifted them to AnyMaybe and joined values at Any, while its api declared lift(r:R). They now lift to Maybe[\R\], the type the api and Set's Intersection already wrote.
224	- A generator's size. Generator declared no size, though three library bodies read one. It now has a default that counts the elements, so "only needs to define the generate method" stays true.
225	#### Specified, but not built
226	- A parameter whose type is left out. The components chapter says type inference finds every type a component leaves out, but no text describes that inference. The checker refused such a parameter at top level and crashed on a local function's. Now the compiled path refuses every such parameter, and the specification says so. This is the one error the checker count shows now.
227	### Where the revival changed the team's own text, and why
228	- The specification. 39 entries in Appendix I, each with a callout at the changed passage. Each change follows one of the resolutions above. The original sentences are quoted with their file and line, and the team's frozen copy is untouched.
229	- The library. The interpreter's library changed most: 3.6K lines added and 2.3K removed since the tag. Each change is either one a resolution above calls for, or a slip the checker refused. The rule is to make each with the library's own devices, as it already does for the same kind of thing.
230	- The team's tests and demos. 43 of their files changed, and none was deleted. The reasons: code meant to wrap now writes the wrapping operators (six tests); SUM is written with its element type; fill's function form is renamed tabulate (seven tests and the demos); numerals and shifts changed in UnsignedTest and two others; the ranges changed in RangePrototype.
231	- Left as the team had it. The grammar, the evaluation model, the algebraic traits, the frozen specification and the full history.
